selected_problem.problem_name: CSF over-drainage causing subdural hematomas and slit ventricle syndrome
selected_problem.problem_statement: CSF shunts drain CSF from the ventricles to a distal compartment (peritoneum, atrium, or venous system). When the pressure differential between the CSF compartment and the distal compartment is too large — particularly when the patient is upright — the shunt drains too much CSF, causing over-drainage. This leads to subdural hematomas (blood pooling between brain and skull), slit ventricle syndrome (ventricles collapse around the catheter), and cranial deformity (especially in pediatric patients). Over-drainage affects 10-20% of shunt patients and is a leading cause of shunt revision surgery.

clinical_evidence.incidence: 10-20% of shunt patients experience over-drainage complications
consequences: Slit ventricle syndrome (causes severe headaches, requires shunt revision)
Cranial deformity (especially in pediatric patients — craniosynostosis-like presentation)
Shunt revision surgery (adds morbidity, infection risk, cost)
clinical_evidence.cost: Each over-drainage complication costs $25K-50K in surgical intervention
clinical_evidence.population: All shunt patients are at risk, but especially: pediatric patients (smaller CSF volume), NPH patients (low-pressure state), and tall patients (larger hydrostatic gradient)

why_existing_solutions_fail.programmable_valves: Programmable valves allow EXTERNAL adjustment of opening pressure, but they CANNOT sense the actual pressure differential in real-time. The physician must guess the right setting based on symptoms. This is REACTIVE, not PROACTIVE.
why_existing_solutions_fail.gravitational_valves: Gravitational valves (e.g., Miethke ProSA) add a gravitational unit that resists flow when upright. But they respond to POSTURE, not to actual venous pressure. They cannot distinguish between 'upright and safe' vs 'upright and over-draining.'
why_existing_solutions_fail.anti_siphon_devices: Anti-siphon devices close when the pressure differential exceeds a threshold. But they use a FIXED threshold — they cannot adapt to patient-specific venous pressure physiology. They also have a risk of UNDER-drainage (blocking flow when drainage is actually needed).

selected_problem.why_eShunt_is_uniquely_positioned: The eShunt creates a CSF→venous pathway. The device is AT the venous interface — it can directly sense venous pressure. VP shunts drain to the peritoneum and have NO access to venous pressure. This means the eShunt can implement a VENOUS-PRESSURE-AWARE regulation mechanism that is physically impossible for VP shunts. The eShunt can measure the actual pressure differential (CSF pressure - venous pressure) and adjust drainage in real-time to prevent over-drainage.
selected_problem.what_new_mechanism_could_solve_it: A venous-pressure-aware flow regulator that: (1) senses venous pressure at the eShunt's venous outflow, (2) computes the actual CSF-to-venous pressure differential, (3) adjusts the drainage rate to maintain a safe differential, (4) prevents over-drainage when the patient is upright (large hydrostatic gradient) while maintaining adequate drainage when the patient is supine (small gradient). This is physically different from gravitational valves (which sense posture, not venous pressure) and from programmable valves (which require external adjustment).

prior_failure.reason: FAILURE_LESSON — reopenable only if new regulation mechanism discovered
prior_failure.what_failed: The prior mechanism failed because it tried to use venous pressure SENSING as the regulation input, but the sensing technology was not adequately differentiated from existing pressure-sensing shunt valves. The prior art search found that venous pressure sensing in shunts was already anticipated.
prior_failure.what_is_different_now: The prior failure was about SENSING venous pressure. The new approach is about USING the eShunt's unique position AT the venous interface to create a MECHANICAL (not electronic) pressure-differential regulator that responds to the actual CSF-to-venous pressure gradient. No electronics, no sensors — just fluid mechanics at the venous interface.
